items.title: Mastering Section 43B(h): Compliance Guide for Payments to Micro and Small Enterprises
items.author: CA Kamal Jain
items.summary: Section 43B(h) of the Income Tax Act mandates that payments to Micro and Small Enterprises must be made within the timeframes specified by the MSMED Act to claim tax deductions on an accrual basis. This guide breaks down the applicability, exceptions, and practical steps businesses must take to avoid disallowed expenses during tax audits.
items.content:
The introduction of clause (h) in Section 43B of the Income Tax Act has fundamentally shifted how businesses manage their accounts payable. Designed to ensure timely payments to Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs), this rule states that any sum payable to an MSE for goods or services will only be allowed as a tax deduction in the year the payment is actually made, unless paid within the time limit set by the MSMED Act, 2006.
With tax audit season approaching, ensuring adherence to this rule is critical to avoid heavy tax liabilities caused by disallowed expenses.

Understanding the Timelines

The MSMED Act, 2006 (Section 15) outlines strict payment deadlines:

With a Written Agreement: Payment must be made within the agreed timeframe, which cannot exceed 45 days from the day of acceptance of the goods or services.

Without a Written Agreement: Payment must be made within 15 days from the day of acceptance.

Non-compliance not only impacts your taxable income but also attracts compound interest under the MSMED Act at three times the bank rate notified by the RBI, which itself is completely disallowed as an income tax deduction. Proper vendor management is no longer just good business practice—it is a strict statutory requirement.

items.title: TDS on Purchase of Property from NRI: Changes from 1 October 2026
items.author: CA Kamal Jain
items.summary: Know the major TDS compliance change from 1 October 2026 when a resident individual or HUF purchases immovable property from an NRI, including the removal of TAN requirement.
items.contentHtml:
TDS on Purchase of Immovable Property from an NRI: Major Compliance Change from 1 October 2026

Effective from 1 October 2026, resident individual and HUF buyers purchasing immovable property from a non-resident seller will receive a significant compliance relief: the requirement to obtain a Tax Deduction and Collection Account Number (TAN) will be removed.

However, the underlying obligation to deduct tax at source (TDS) on payments to a non-resident seller continues to apply.

This distinction is important for buyers, property consultants, legal professionals and tax professionals involved in transactions where an NRI/non-resident is selling immovable property situated in India.

1. What is changing from 1 October 2026?

Under the existing framework, when a resident individual or HUF purchases immovable property from a non-resident seller, the buyer is required to comply with the TDS provisions applicable to payments to a non-resident and obtain a TAN.

The Finance Act, 2026 introduces a specific relaxation.

With effect from 1 October 2026, a resident individual or HUF deducting tax on consideration paid for the transfer of immovable property from a non-resident will not be required to obtain TAN for that transaction.

The amendment has been made to section 397 of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

In simple terms

Earlier:

Purchase property from NRI → TDS obligation + TAN requirement

From 1 October 2026:

Purchase property from NRI → TDS obligation continues, but TAN requirement is removed for an eligible resident individual/HUF buyer.

The Income Tax Department has specifically stated that the objective is to reduce the compliance burden associated with obtaining TAN for what may be a single property transaction.

2. What is NOT changing?

The most important point is that TDS itself has not been abolished.

The relaxation is regarding TAN, not the underlying requirement to deduct tax.

Where a non-resident sells immovable property in India, the payment falls under the provisions applicable to payments to non-residents. Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, section 393(2) deals with specified payments to non-residents.

Therefore, a buyer should not interpret the October 2026 amendment as:

"TDS is no longer applicable when buying property from an NRI."

That interpretation would be incorrect.

The correct understanding is:

TDS continues to apply; the eligible resident individual/HUF buyer will simply no longer need TAN for the transaction from 1 October 2026.

3. Why is this important for NRI property transactions?

There is an important distinction between purchasing property from a resident seller and purchasing property from a non-resident seller.

For a resident seller, the property TDS mechanism historically operated under section 194-IA, subject to the prescribed conditions and threshold.

For a non-resident seller, the transaction is dealt with under the provisions applicable to payments to non-residents.

The Income Tax Department confirms that when a non-resident sells immovable property in India, the buyer is responsible for deducting TDS.

This means that determining the seller's residential status is a critical first step before deciding the applicable TDS compliance mechanism.

4. Is there a ₹50 lakh threshold for an NRI seller?

This is an area where buyers should exercise particular caution.

The ₹50 lakh threshold associated with the standard property TDS provision for a resident seller should not simply be applied to an NRI transaction.

The Income Tax Department's guidance distinguishes transactions involving resident and non-resident sellers and states that payments to a non-resident seller are subject to the provisions applicable to non-residents.

Accordingly, a buyer should not assume that a property can be purchased from an NRI without TDS merely because the sale consideration is below ₹50 lakh.

The residential status of the seller must first be established.

5. How is TDS determined when an NRI sells property?

The tax treatment of the NRI seller depends upon the nature of the capital gain and the applicable provisions.

For example, the Income Tax Department currently states that for transfers by a non-resident:

Long-term capital gain

For property held for more than 24 months, the applicable base tax rate for transfers on or after 23 July 2024 is generally 12.5%, subject to the applicable provisions, surcharge and health and education cess.

Short-term capital gain

Where the property is held for 24 months or less, the applicable rate can generally be 30% for an individual/firm or 35% for a foreign company, subject to the applicable provisions.

The final TDS treatment can also depend upon factors such as the seller's status, applicable surcharge and cess, lower/nil deduction certificate and applicable tax treaty provisions.

Important: The actual amount of TDS in an NRI property transaction should therefore be determined transaction-by-transaction rather than applying a blanket percentage without examining the facts.

6. What was the compliance position before 1 October 2026?

For a resident individual/HUF purchasing immovable property from a non-resident, the buyer was required to obtain TAN for the purpose of deducting tax.

This created an additional compliance step, particularly where an individual was involved in only one property transaction.

The Finance Act, 2026 specifically identifies this burden and removes the TAN requirement for eligible resident individuals and HUFs from 1 October 2026.

7. What will the process look like from 1 October 2026?

From 1 October 2026, an eligible resident individual/HUF purchasing immovable property from a non-resident will be able to deduct TDS without obtaining TAN for that transaction.

The buyer will use the PAN-based mechanism prescribed by the Income Tax Department.

The Finance Act 2026 amendment provides the TAN relaxation through section 397, while the corresponding TDS obligation continues under the relevant provisions.

The Income Tax Department has also explained that the objective is to make the deduction and reporting process similar to the PAN-based mechanism used for specified property transactions.

8. Form 141 and the new PAN-based reporting mechanism

The Income Tax Department has introduced Form 141, a unified challan-cum-statement mechanism under the Income-tax Act, 2025.

Form 141 consolidates the earlier PAN-based challan-cum-statement forms, including Form 26QB, and contains a specific schedule for TDS on transfer of immovable property.

For property transactions covered by the new PAN-based mechanism, Schedule B of Form 141 deals with:

TDS on transfer of immovable property.

The form requires transaction information such as:

  • Type of immovable property

  • Property address

  • Agreement date

  • Date of payment/credit

  • Amount paid or credited

  • Amount on which tax is liable to be deducted

  • Applicable rate

  • Amount of TDS

  • Date of deduction

  • Tax deposit details

The exact applicability of the form should be checked against the transaction date, seller status and applicable provisions.

9. What should a buyer check before purchasing property from an NRI?

Before executing the transaction, the buyer should verify the following:

1. Residential status of the seller

Confirm whether the seller is actually a non-resident for income-tax purposes.

This is fundamental because the TDS mechanism differs depending upon the seller's residential status.

2. PAN of the seller

The seller's valid PAN should be obtained and verified.

3. Property ownership documents

The buyer should verify the title and ownership documents before proceeding with the transaction.

4. Acquisition date and cost

The seller's acquisition details may be relevant for determining the nature and tax treatment of the capital gain.

5. Holding period

Determine whether the transaction results in long-term or short-term capital gains.

6. Lower/Nil deduction certificate

If the seller has obtained an applicable lower or nil deduction certificate, the buyer should verify its validity and conditions before applying the reduced rate.

7. Applicable TDS rate

The rate should be determined after considering:

  • Nature of capital gain

  • Seller's status

  • Applicable provisions

  • Surcharge

  • Health and education cess

  • DTAA considerations, wherever applicable

  • Any valid lower/nil deduction certificate

8. Agreement and payment structure

The TDS implications should be considered before making an advance or instalment payment.

10. Example

Suppose:

Buyer: Resident Individual
Seller: NRI
Property: Residential property situated in India
Transaction date: 15 October 2026

Under the amended framework applicable from 1 October 2026:

TDS obligation: Continues to apply.

TAN requirement for the resident individual buyer: Relaxed for the qualifying transaction.

Therefore, the buyer should not conclude that no TDS is required merely because TAN is no longer required.

Instead, the buyer should determine the applicable TDS rate and complete the prescribed PAN-based deduction and reporting process.

11. What if the buyer is a company or another non-individual?

The October 2026 relaxation specifically refers to a resident individual or Hindu undivided family.

Therefore, it should not automatically be extended to every category of buyer.

A company, firm, LLP or other entity purchasing property from an NRI should independently examine its TAN and TDS compliance requirements.

The statutory language of the amendment specifically identifies the resident individual/HUF category.

12. Key takeaway

The change from 1 October 2026 can be summarised in one sentence:

For an eligible resident individual or HUF purchasing immovable property from a non-resident, TAN will no longer be required for deducting TDS, but the TDS obligation itself continues.

Therefore, buyers should not confuse:

Removal of TAN requirement

with

Removal of TDS requirement.

They are two different compliance matters.

Quick Comparison

ParticularBefore 1 October 2026From 1 October 2026
Resident individual/HUF buys property from NRITDS applicableTDS applicable
TAN requirement for eligible resident individual/HUFRequiredNot required
TDS obligationApplicableContinues
PAN-based complianceLimited/subject to applicable mechanismIntroduced/expanded for the specified transaction
Need to determine correct TDS rateYesYes
Need to verify seller's residential statusYesYes

Practical Advice for Buyers

A property transaction involving an NRI should not be treated as an ordinary property purchase merely because the buyer is an individual.

Before making any payment, the buyer should determine:

Seller status → Applicable TDS provision → Applicable rate → Lower/Nil deduction possibility → TDS deduction → Deposit/reporting → Documentation

Early tax planning is particularly important because an error in the TDS process can create additional interest, fee, penalty and other compliance consequences.

For high-value property transactions, buyers and sellers should obtain professional tax advice before the payment schedule is finalised.

Conclusion

The Finance Act, 2026 has introduced an important compliance simplification for resident individuals and HUFs purchasing immovable property from non-resident sellers.

From 1 October 2026, such eligible buyers will no longer be required to obtain TAN solely for deducting TDS on the qualifying property transaction.

However, the tax deduction obligation remains.

Accordingly, the correct interpretation of the amendment is:

"TAN removed — TDS not removed."

Buyers should therefore focus on correctly determining the applicable TDS provisions, rate, deduction point and reporting requirements rather than treating the amendment as an exemption from TDS.

Disclaimer: This article is intended for general informational purposes and is based on the provisions and official guidance available as of September 2026. Tax laws, rules, forms and procedural requirements may be amended or updated. The applicability of TDS in an individual transaction depends on its specific facts and circumstances. Professional advice should be obtained before completing a significant property transaction.

items.title: Rule 46(8): India-Based Backup of Electronic Books – Practical Challenges
items.author: CA Hitesh Jain
items.summary: Rule 46(8) of the Income-tax Rules, 2026 mandates that businesses maintaining electronic books of account must keep them accessible in India and maintain daily backups on servers physically located within the country.
items.contentHtml:
The growing use of cloud-based accounting and ERP systems has made electronic maintenance of books of account the norm rather than the exception. Rule 46(8) of the Income-tax Rules, 2026 introduces an important compliance requirement for taxpayers maintaining prescribed books and documents electronically: the records must remain accessible in India, and their backup must be maintained daily on servers physically located in India.

While the objective of the provision is understandable from the perspective of tax administration and availability of records, its implementation may present several practical challenges for businesses.
Real-Life Problems

1. Uncertainty regarding physical server location

Most businesses use cloud platforms where data is distributed across multiple data centres. The taxpayer may have access to the data from India without knowing where the backup is physically stored. Obtaining a clear confirmation of the physical location of backup servers from global cloud providers may itself be difficult.

2. Global ERP systems

Large multinational companies commonly use a single global ERP system. The database and disaster-recovery infrastructure may be located outside India as part of the group’s global IT architecture. Creating a separate India-based backup solely for Indian tax purposes may involve significant technical and financial costs.

3. Daily backup is not as simple as it sounds

The requirement for a daily backup raises practical questions: What exactly constitutes a daily backup? Should every transaction entered during the day be backed up? What happens if the automated backup fails? Who will monitor and document such failures?

A taxpayer may therefore need a formal monitoring and exception-reporting mechanism.

4. Third-party service providers

Many businesses outsource accounting and IT functions. A company may have little direct control over the servers used by its accounting service provider or cloud vendor. Merely obtaining an assurance that “data is secure” may not establish compliance with a specific statutory requirement concerning the physical location of servers.

5. Cost of compliance for smaller businesses

For large enterprises, India-based backup infrastructure may be technically feasible. For smaller businesses and professional firms using inexpensive cloud accounting applications, however, maintaining a separate India-based backup system could create additional cost and administrative burden.

6. Data accessibility versus data location

A particularly important distinction is that accessibility from India and physical storage in India are not the same thing. A business may be able to access its books instantly from an office in India while the actual backup is stored overseas. This distinction could become a significant area of scrutiny.

Practical Way Forward

Businesses maintaining electronic books should consider:

* identifying all systems in which prescribed books are maintained;
* obtaining confirmation of the location of backup servers;
* ensuring daily backups;
* maintaining backup logs and evidence;
* reviewing contracts with cloud and accounting-service providers; and
* periodically testing restoration of backed-up records.

Conclusion

Rule 46(8) is a significant development in the digitalisation of tax compliance. However, its practical implementation may be challenging, particularly for businesses dependent on global cloud infrastructure.

The real issue is not simply whether a taxpayer has a backup, but whether the taxpayer can demonstrate that the backup is maintained daily and on servers physically located in India.

For tax professionals, this provision therefore creates a new area of interaction between tax compliance, accounting systems and IT infrastructure. Businesses should address the issue proactively rather than waiting until their electronic records are required during assessment or verification proceedings
